messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Leilani is a 46-year-old forensic analyst, a woman whose professional life had always been built on order, pattern recognition, and the quiet certainty of evidence. She came to therapy at the urging of her husband, who had grown increasingly alarmed by the changes he saw in her over the past eight months. She sat in the chair across from me with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her gaze fixed on a spot on the floor. She spoke in a flat, measured tone, as if she were delivering a lab report, but her voice dropped to a whisper when she reached the part she had been dreading to say aloud.

The traumatic event occurred on a Tuesday afternoon in early spring. Leilani’s younger brother, Koa, had been a commercial diver, a man who spent his life working in the deep, dark waters off the coast of Alaska. He had called her the night before, laughing about a seal that had stolen his glove, and she had laughed too, telling him to be careful. The next day, a supervisor called her at her desk. There had been an accident. A sudden equipment failure during a deep-water repair. Koa was gone before anyone could reach him. Leilani did not see his body. She did not hear his voice again. What she did hear, and what she could not stop hearing, was the sound of the supervisor’s voice on the phone—the way his words had stopped and started, the hollow silence between each sentence. That voice lived inside her now. It would return without warning, usually at night when the house was quiet, and she would hear it again, word for word, as if the call were happening in real time. When the memory came, it was not a story with a beginning and an end. It was a snapshot: the grey afternoon light through her office window, the phone pressed to her ear, the supervisor’s voice saying *there’s no easy way to say this*. That single image, frozen and unbearable, would flood her with a wave of emotion so overwhelming that she had to stop whatever she was doing—sometimes mid-sentence, sometimes mid-step—and press her palms against her eyes until it passed.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani’s world contracted. She had always taken pride in her work, in the meticulous analysis of digital evidence that helped build cases, but now the thought of sitting at her desk made her chest tighten. She began to avoid it. She would arrive late, leave early, or call in sick on days when she knew a case file would require sustained concentration. Her supervisor noticed. A colleague had to take over a major project. Leilani told herself it was just a temporary thing, that she needed a break, but she knew, deep down, that she was afraid. Afraid that the phone would ring again. Afraid that the snapshot would return while she was trying to focus. She stopped eating properly. She would go the entire day on black coffee, telling herself she wasn’t hungry, and then at night, when the house was finally still, she would stay awake until two or three in the morning, scrolling through news articles about diving accidents, reading comments from strangers, searching for something she could not name. Her husband would find her in the living room, the laptop glowing in the dark, and she would close it quickly, saying she couldn’t sleep.

What frightened Leilani most was not the memory itself, but what it had done to her sense of the world. She had lost her faith. Not in God—she had never been particularly religious—but in the basic assumption that life made sense. She had believed, without ever saying it aloud, that if you worked hard and loved your people and stayed careful, you would be safe. Koa’s death had shattered that belief. Now she saw the world as a place where the worst thing could happen at any moment, for no reason, and there was nothing you could do to stop it. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. She had stopped looking forward to things. She went through the motions at work, at home, in conversations with her husband, but she felt hollow, as if the person she used to be had been erased. She said to me, in a voice that was barely audible, “My life has been destroyed by this. I don’t know what’s left.”

She came to therapy because her husband had told her, gently but firmly, that he could not watch her disappear any longer. She was not sure she wanted to get better. She was not sure she deserved to. But she was tired—so tired of the snapshots and the voice and the long, sleepless hours—and she was afraid that if she did not try something, she would lose what little she had left. What she hoped for, she said, was not to forget Koa, but to stop feeling like his death had taken her with him.
